definition: To make a machine start working, or to be the motive that drives someone to act.
examples: The valve is *actuated* by a small electric motor.
He insisted he was *actuated* by loyalty, not money.
hook: Latin actus 'a doing' — the same root as act and actual.

definition: Clever and skilful, especially at handling people or tricky situations.
examples: She gave an *adroit* answer that dodged the question without seeming evasive.
He's *adroit* at steering meetings back on track.
hook: French à droit, 'to the right' — the right hand was the skilful one. Its opposite is gauche, 'left'.
openers: That was an adroit bit of parking.
You handled that client call pretty adroitly.
Adroit move, changing the subject before he asked about the deadline.

definition: Friendly, relaxed and easy to talk to.
examples: The new manager is *affable* and remembers everyone's name.
He chatted *affably* with the waiter about the footy.
hook: Latin affabilis, 'easy to speak to' — from fari, 'to speak'.
openers: Your dad's very affable — he talked to me for an hour.
The barista's always so affable, even at 7am.
He seems affable enough, but I wouldn't lend him money.

definition: A fossil of an extinct sea creature with a flat, coiled, spiral shell.
examples: We found a perfect *ammonite* in the cliffs at Lyme Regis.
The paperweight on her desk is a polished *ammonite*.
hook: Named after the Egyptian god Ammon, whose curled ram's horns the shells resemble.

definition: To pay off a debt, or spread out the cost of something, in regular instalments over time.
examples: The loan is *amortized* over thirty years.
We *amortize* the cost of the laptops across three years.
hook: Old French amortir, 'to kill' — you kill off the debt bit by bit.
openers: If you amortize the gym membership over a year it's only two bucks a session.
I'm amortizing this coffee machine — every cup at home is a saving.

definition: The direct opposite of something.
examples: His messy desk is the *antithesis* of her minimalist one.
Fast food is the *antithesis* of everything this restaurant stands for.
hook: Greek anti 'against' + thesis 'placing' — something set against the original.
openers: This weather is the antithesis of a beach day.
My sister's the antithesis of me — she plans everything.
Group assignments are the antithesis of fun.

definition: A food, drink or drug said to increase sexual desire.
examples: Oysters are famously supposed to be an *aphrodisiac*.
Apparently, for him, confidence is the ultimate *aphrodisiac*.
hook: From Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love.
openers: They say power's the ultimate aphrodisiac.
Is dark chocolate actually an aphrodisiac or is that marketing?

definition: The highest point or most perfect example of something.
examples: This dish is the *apotheosis* of Sunday comfort food.
The final album was the *apotheosis* of their sound.
hook: Greek apotheoun, 'to make into a god' — raising something to divine status.
openers: This burger is the apotheosis of pub food.
That last-minute goal was the apotheosis of the whole season.

definition: With reference to; or (as an adjective) appropriate to the moment.
examples: *Apropos* of nothing, she asked if I'd ever been to Peru.
His comment was surprisingly *apropos*.
hook: French à propos, 'to the purpose'.
openers: Apropos of nothing — has anyone seen my charger?
Apropos the trip, did we ever book the car?
That song is very apropos given the weather.

definition: Like an eagle — usually describing a nose that is hooked or curved.
examples: He had an *aquiline* nose and sharp grey eyes.
Roman busts often show strong, *aquiline* profiles.
hook: Latin aquila, 'eagle' — a nose hooked like an eagle's beak.
openers: He's got that aquiline profile, like a Roman emperor.
Everyone in her family has the same aquiline nose.

definition: The weapons and military equipment of an army or country.
examples: The ship carried heavy *armaments*.
Both countries agreed to limit their nuclear *armaments*.
hook: Latin arma, 'weapons' — the same root as arms and army.

definition: A large, tall cupboard or wardrobe, often antique and ornate.
examples: The bedroom had an old oak *armoire* instead of a built-in wardrobe.
We found a painted *armoire* at the market.
hook: French, from Latin armarium — originally a cupboard for storing weapons and tools.
openers: Where did you get that armoire? It's amazing.
My clothes don't fit in a wardrobe anymore — I need an armoire.

definition: A place of religious retreat in India, or a community where people live and study under a spiritual teacher.
examples: She spent three months at an *ashram* in Rishikesh.
The commune was run like an *ashram*.
hook: Sanskrit āśrama, 'hermitage' — a place of religious effort.

definition: Showing great care and steady effort; thorough and persistent.
examples: Thanks to her *assiduous* note-taking, nothing got missed.
He *assiduously* avoided talking about politics at dinner.
hook: Latin assidere, 'to sit beside' — someone who sits down to a task and stays there.
openers: You've been very assiduous with the gym lately.
I assiduously avoided the washing up all week.
Credit to her — she was assiduous about checking every reference.

definition: Suggesting that things will go well; a good sign for the future.
examples: Rain on the first day wasn't an *auspicious* start to the holiday.
They chose an *auspicious* date for the wedding.
hook: Latin auspex — a priest who read omens from watching birds fly (avis 'bird' + specere 'look').
openers: Burning the toast isn't an auspicious start to the day.
Free parking right out front — auspicious.
Not the most auspicious first date, but we're still talking.

definition: Kind, friendly and a bit protective, like a favourite uncle.
examples: The coach had an *avuncular* way of giving feedback.
He put an *avuncular* arm around the new guy's shoulders.
hook: Latin avunculus, 'mother's brother' — your uncle.
openers: The new supervisor's very avuncular — I like him.
He gets all avuncular whenever someone mentions uni.
Bit of an avuncular pat on the back there.

definition: Very elaborate and decorated — originally the grand style of 17th-century European art and music; now also anything overly complicated.
examples: The church has a *baroque* ceiling covered in gold.
The tax rules have become positively *baroque*.
hook: Portuguese barroco, 'misshapen pearl'.
openers: This menu is a bit baroque — I just want a burger.
The approval process at work is absolutely baroque.

definition: A small corner shop selling groceries (especially in New York), or a wine cellar or bar in Spain.
examples: He grabbed a sandwich from the *bodega* on the corner.
We spent the evening in a tiny *bodega* in Seville.
hook: Spanish, from Greek apothēkē 'storehouse' — the same root as apothecary.
openers: This servo is basically a bodega with petrol.
I want one of those New York bodega sandwiches.

definition: A citizen of a town, especially a respectable, well-off, middle-class one.
examples: The town's *burghers* built grand houses along the canal.
The festival scandalised the respectable *burghers*.
hook: Dutch burger, 'citizen of a borough'.

definition: Entertainment such as singing, dancing or comedy performed in a nightclub or restaurant while the audience eats and drinks.
examples: They saw a *cabaret* show in Berlin.
The bar turns into a *cabaret* venue on Fridays.
hook: Old French cabaret, 'small tavern'.

definition: A false statement made to damage someone's reputation, or the act of making such statements.
examples: She was the victim of vicious *calumny* in the press.
His *calumniators* never produced any proof.
hook: Latin calumnia, 'trickery, false accusation'.
openers: That's pure calumny — I never ate your leftovers.
Spreading calumny about the group chat admin, are we?

definition: The old walled part of a North African city, often with a fortress and narrow winding streets.
examples: We got lost in the *casbah* of Algiers.
The *casbah* sits on the hill above the port.
hook: Arabic qaṣaba, 'citadel'. Also spelled kasbah.

definition: To criticise or tell someone off severely.
examples: The report *castigated* the council for wasting money.
She *castigated* herself for forgetting his birthday.
hook: Latin castigare, 'to correct', from castus 'pure' — literally 'to make pure'.
openers: I got castigated for leaving one mug in the sink.
Don't castigate yourself — everyone misses a deadline.
The reviews absolutely castigated that movie.

definition: King of the Franks (c. 742–814) who united much of Western Europe and was crowned the first Holy Roman Emperor.
examples: *Charlemagne* was crowned emperor on Christmas Day in the year 800.
hook: Old French for 'Charles the Great' (Latin Carolus Magnus).

definition: Strong contrast between light and dark, especially in a painting, photo or film.
examples: Caravaggio was a master of *chiaroscuro*.
The film's moody *chiaroscuro* makes every scene look like a painting.
hook: Italian chiaro 'light' + scuro 'dark'.
openers: The lighting in this bar is very chiaroscuro.
Great photo — love the chiaroscuro from that window.

definition: To become thick or solid as it cools, like fat or blood; or for ideas to take shape.
examples: The gravy had *congealed* in the pan.
Slowly, a plan began to *congeal*.
hook: Latin congelare, 'to freeze together' — related to gelid and gelato.
openers: Eat your pasta before the cheese congeals.
My brain has completely congealed after that lecture.

definition: Easy to notice; attracting attention.
examples: He felt *conspicuous* in a suit when everyone else wore shorts.
There was a *conspicuous* absence of thank-yous.
hook: Latin conspicere, 'to look at closely'.
openers: The boss was conspicuously absent from the Friday drinks.
I'm going to be very conspicuous in this hi-vis jacket.
That's a conspicuous lack of washing up, guys.

definition: A sudden, violent shaking of the body; or a violent upheaval in society. In the plural, uncontrollable laughter.
examples: The fever brought on *convulsions*.
The audience was in *convulsions* by the end of the set.
hook: Latin convellere, 'to tear up, wrench'.
openers: That video had me in convulsions.
The whole room went into convulsions when he tripped.

definition: An offensive, dated term for an unskilled labourer from Asia, especially in the colonial era.
examples: The novel uses the colonial term *coolie*, which is now considered a slur.
hook: Probably from Hindi qulī, 'hired labourer'.

definition: Something or someone excellent or remarkable (informal).
examples: That was a *corker* of a game.
Her speech was an absolute *corker*.
hook: Possibly from cork — something so good it puts a cork in the argument.
openers: That was a corker of a weekend.
This pie is an absolute corker.
Your nan's a corker — she's hilarious.

definition: Sparkling or flashing; or (of talk and wit) brilliantly clever and lively.
examples: The play is full of *coruscating* dialogue.
He delivered a *coruscating* attack on the policy.
hook: Latin coruscare, 'to glitter, flash'.
openers: That was a coruscating review — she destroyed it.
Thanks for the coruscating wit at 8am.

definition: Including people and influences from many countries; or (of a person) worldly and well-travelled.
examples: Melbourne is a wonderfully *cosmopolitan* city.
She has a *cosmopolitan* outlook from growing up in four countries.
hook: Greek kosmos 'world' + politēs 'citizen' — a citizen of the world.
openers: Very cosmopolitan of you, ordering in Italian.
This street's gotten so cosmopolitan — there's food from everywhere.
He's gone all cosmopolitan since his exchange semester.

definition: A wild European plant with clusters of small, sweet-smelling yellow flowers in spring.
examples: The meadow was full of *cowslips* in April.
She made wine from *cowslips*.
hook: Old English cūslyppe — literally 'cow dung', since it grew in cow pastures.

definition: A set of beliefs or principles that guide how someone lives or works.
examples: 'Leave it better than you found it' is his *credo*.
The company's *credo* is printed on every mug.
hook: Latin 'I believe' — the first word of the Christian creed.
openers: 'Never skip leg day' — that's my credo.
My credo for group projects: start early, trust no one.
What's your credo when it comes to leftovers?

definition: A mild, informal swear word used instead of 'damn'.
examples: *Dang*, I left my keys at home.
hook: A polite stand-in for 'damn'.

definition: To melt or dissolve into liquid (especially by absorbing moisture from the air); figuratively, to fade or dissolve away.
examples: The salt *deliquesced* in the humid air.
His confidence *deliquesced* the moment she walked in.
hook: Latin deliquescere, 'to melt away' — from liquere, 'to be liquid'.

definition: A severe flood or downpour; or an overwhelming number of things arriving at once.
examples: We got caught in a *deluge* on the walk home.
After the post went viral, she was *deluged* with messages.
hook: Latin diluvium, 'flood' — from diluere, 'to wash away'.
openers: Bring an umbrella, it's a deluge out there.
I came back from leave to a deluge of emails.
We've been deluged with zucchinis from Mum's garden.

definition: Winning support by stirring up people's emotions and prejudices rather than using reasoned argument.
examples: The campaign descended into pure *demagoguery*.
He's a *demagogue* who blames every problem on outsiders.
hook: Greek dēmos 'people' + agōgos 'leader' — a 'leader of the people' who whips up the mob.
openers: That speech was textbook demagoguery.
Bit of demagoguery from you there — rallying the house against the dishwasher.
I can't watch the debates, it's all demagoguery now.

definition: A prefix meaning 'half' or 'partly', as in demigod or demi-glace.
examples: Hercules was a *demi*god — half human, half divine.
hook: French demi, from Latin dimidius, 'half'.

definition: Not matching or agreeing; inconsistent with something else.
examples: The two witnesses gave *discrepant* accounts.
The numbers in the report were wildly *discrepant*.
hook: Latin discrepare, 'to sound different' — two stories that don't harmonise. The source of discrepancy.
openers: Our memories of that night are very discrepant.
The bank statement and my maths are a bit discrepant.

definition: To refuse to have anything more to do with someone or something.
examples: His parents threatened to *disown* him.
hook: Simply dis- + own: to stop owning up to.

definition: Someone who openly opposes an official policy, especially of an authoritarian state.
examples: The regime imprisoned dozens of *dissidents*.
She was a *dissident* voice on the committee.
hook: Latin dissidere, 'to sit apart'.
openers: I'm the lone dissident on pineapple pizza in this house.
There's always one dissident in the group chat when we pick a restaurant.

definition: Silly, forgetful or scatterbrained in a harmless way (informal; can sound patronising).
examples: I had a *ditsy* moment and put the milk in the cupboard.
The character is a *ditsy* but lovable receptionist.
hook: 1970s American slang, origin unknown — perhaps a blend of dizzy and dotty. Also spelled ditzy.
openers: Sorry, ditsy moment — I've walked in here and forgotten why.
I'm being very ditsy today, I've lost my phone twice.
Don't mind me, I'm a bit ditsy before coffee.

definition: A belief or set of beliefs that people are expected to accept without question.
examples: Question the *dogma* that you need eight glasses of water a day.
The party line had hardened into *dogma*.
hook: Greek dogma, 'opinion' — from dokein, 'to seem good'.
openers: 'No carbs after six' is just diet dogma.
You're being very dogmatic about the dishwasher stacking.
There's a lot of dogma about how to brew coffee.

definition: A man who seduces lots of women; a womaniser.
examples: He fancies himself a bit of a *Don Juan*.
Her ex was a real *Don Juan* — charming and unreliable.
hook: A legendary Spanish seducer from a 1630 play — later Byron's poem and Mozart's opera Don Giovanni.
openers: Look at you, the Don Juan of the dog park.
He's a total Don Juan — three dates this week.
Easy there, Don Juan.

definition: Funny in an odd or dry, understated way.
examples: He has a *droll* sense of humour.
'Lovely weather,' she said *drolly*, as the rain poured down.
hook: French drôle, 'funny, odd'.
openers: Very droll — you should do stand-up.
I love her droll little comments in meetings.
Oh, how droll — the printer's jammed again.

definition: Threats or pressure used to make someone do something against their will.
examples: The confession was made under *duress*.
She only agreed to karaoke under *duress*.
hook: Old French duresse, 'hardness' — from Latin durus, 'hard' (as in durable).
openers: I'm only going to this wedding under duress.
Any compliments I gave the cooking were under duress.
He agreed to the hike, but under duress.

definition: Relating to the Christian Church or its clergy.
examples: The library holds rare *ecclesiastical* manuscripts.
He wore *ecclesiastical* robes for the ceremony.
hook: Greek ekklēsia, 'assembly' — the gathering of the faithful, later the church itself.

definition: A large, imposing building; or a complex system of ideas built up over time.
examples: The bank's headquarters is a grand stone *edifice*.
The whole *edifice* of his argument rested on one bad statistic.
hook: Latin aedificium, 'building' — from aedes 'dwelling' + facere 'make'. Same root as edify ('build up').
openers: Have you seen the new apartment block? What an edifice.
My whole excuse was an edifice built on sand.

definition: How well something works or produces the result it's meant to.
examples: There's little evidence for the *efficacy* of the supplement.
I'm starting to doubt the *efficacy* of my alarm clock.
hook: Latin efficax, 'powerful, effective'.
openers: I question the efficacy of these 'blue light' glasses.
What's the efficacy of a nap versus a coffee?
The efficacy of my New Year's resolutions is about zero.

definition: Shameless, cheeky boldness; insolent nerve.
examples: He had the *effrontery* to ask for a raise after missing the deadline.
Her *effrontery* left the whole table speechless.
hook: Late Latin effrons, 'shameless' — literally 'without a forehead', i.e. unable to blush.
openers: The effrontery of the seagull that stole my chips.
You have the effrontery to eat the last Tim Tam?
What effrontery — he's asking for a lift after not paying me back.

definition: Believing that all people are equal and deserve the same rights and opportunities.
examples: The company has a flat, *egalitarian* structure.
Australia likes to think of itself as an *egalitarian* society.
hook: French égal, 'equal'.
openers: Let's be egalitarian and split the bill evenly.
Very egalitarian of you to give everyone the same size slice.
The office is pretty egalitarian — the CEO sits with everyone.

definition: Someone who quietly holds power and influence behind the scenes, without an official title.
examples: The chief of staff was the real *éminence grise* of the government.
She's the *éminence grise* of the department — nothing happens without her.
hook: French 'grey eminence' — nickname of Father Joseph, the grey-robed adviser behind Cardinal Richelieu.
openers: The office manager is the real éminence grise around here.
Your mum's clearly the éminence grise of family Christmas.

definition: To give someone or something greater dignity or worth; or to make someone a noble.
examples: Hard work, she believed, *ennobles* the spirit.
He was *ennobled* for his services to science.
hook: en- 'make' + noble.
openers: Doing the dishes does not ennoble the soul, whatever Mum says.
Don't try to ennoble a takeaway dinner by putting it on a nice plate.

definition: Lasting for only a very short time.
examples: Fame on social media is *ephemeral*.
The cherry blossom's beauty is *ephemeral* — a week, then gone.
hook: Greek ephēmeros, 'lasting only a day' — epi 'on' + hēmera 'day'.
openers: My motivation to go running is very ephemeral.
Enjoy this sunshine, it's ephemeral.
Trends on TikTok are so ephemeral.

definition: Pale and weak from lack of light (of a plant); or feeble and lacking vigour (of a person or thing).
examples: The seedlings in the cupboard were *etiolated* and yellow.
After a month of exams he looked thin and *etiolated*.
hook: French étioler, 'to blanch' — what happens to plants grown in the dark.

definition: Showing that someone is not guilty or not to blame.
examples: The defence found *exculpatory* evidence on the CCTV.
The receipt was *exculpatory* — I'd paid after all.
hook: Latin ex 'out of' + culpa 'blame' (as in mea culpa).
openers: I have exculpatory evidence — the dog ate it, here's the photo.
The group chat is very exculpatory, I said I'd be late.

definition: To take property away from its owner, especially by a government for public use.
examples: The land was *expropriated* to build a highway.
Someone has *expropriated* my favourite mug.
hook: Latin ex 'out of' + proprium 'property'.
openers: Who expropriated my phone charger?
The cat has expropriated my side of the bed.

definition: An exact copy or reproduction of something.
examples: The museum displays a *facsimile* of the original manuscript.
The restaurant is a *facsimile* of a 1950s diner.
hook: Latin fac simile, 'make similar' — the origin of 'fax'.
openers: This 'Italian' pasta is a poor facsimile of the real thing.
My attempt at Mum's lasagne was a reasonable facsimile.

definition: An embarrassing social mistake.
examples: Wearing white to a wedding is a classic *faux pas*.
I committed a *faux pas* by calling her by my ex's name.
hook: French 'false step'.
openers: Is it a faux pas to bring store-bought dessert?
Bit of a faux pas, replying-all to that email.
Socks with sandals — major faux pas.

definition: The ability to produce many offspring or new growth; or a great productiveness of ideas.
examples: The *fecundity* of the soil made the valley rich.
Her creative *fecundity* is astonishing — three novels in two years.
hook: Latin fecundus, 'fruitful'.
openers: The fecundity of this zucchini plant is out of control.
Love the fecundity of ideas in this brainstorm.

definition: Faithfulness to a person, cause or belief; or how accurately something is copied or reproduced.
examples: The film shows great *fidelity* to the book.
Her *fidelity* to the team never wavered.
hook: Latin fides, 'faith' — the dog's name Fido is Latin for 'I trust'.
openers: The fidelity of that cover song is uncanny.
My fidelity to this café is unshakeable.

definition: Relating to, or expected of, a son or daughter.
examples: He visited every Sunday out of *filial* duty.
Confucian ethics place great weight on *filial* piety.
hook: Latin filius 'son' / filia 'daughter'.
openers: I'm calling Mum tonight — filial duty.
Washing Dad's car counts as my filial contribution for the month.

definition: Sex between people who are not married to each other (a formal or religious term).
examples: The preacher railed against drinking, gambling and *fornication*.
Old laws punished *fornication* with fines or public shaming.
hook: Latin fornix, 'arch, vault' — Roman brothels were in vaulted cellars.

definition: Spanish for a friar or monk.
examples: The old *fraile* rang the monastery bell at dawn.
hook: Spanish, from Latin frater, 'brother' — related to friar and fraternal.

definition: Done secretly or quietly to avoid being noticed, often guiltily.
examples: He cast a *furtive* glance at his phone during the meeting.
She *furtively* slipped a biscuit into her pocket.
hook: Latin furtivus, 'stolen' — from fur, 'thief'.
openers: I saw that furtive look at the dessert menu.
Why are you being so furtive? What did you buy?
The dog's been very furtive since the bin got knocked over.

definition: Awkward and lacking social grace or tact.
examples: It felt a bit *gauche* to mention the price of the gift.
As a teenager he was shy and *gauche*.
hook: French 'left' — the left hand was the clumsy one. The opposite of adroit ('to the right').
openers: Is it gauche to ask how much they paid for the house?
Sorry, that was a bit gauche of me.
Talking about salary at dinner feels gauche.

definition: Extremely cold; icy.
examples: We dived into the *gelid* water of the mountain lake.
She gave him a *gelid* stare.
hook: Latin gelidus, from gelu 'frost' — the same family as gelato and congeal.
openers: The office air-con is absolutely gelid.
That ocean was gelid — I lasted thirty seconds.

definition: To make lots of gestures with your hands and arms while talking, often excitedly.
examples: He *gesticulated* wildly as he described the near-miss.
Two drivers stood in the road, *gesticulating* at each other.
hook: Latin gesticulus, 'little gesture'.
openers: Stop gesticulating with the knife, you'll take someone's eye out.
He gesticulates so much when he talks about footy.
I can tell it's a good story from how much you're gesticulating.

definition: Done without good reason; unnecessary or uncalled for.
examples: The film has some *gratuitous* violence.
That was a *gratuitous* dig at his cooking.
hook: Latin gratuitus, 'freely given' — free, and therefore uncalled for.
openers: That was a gratuitous amount of cheese — I love it.
Bit of a gratuitous jab at my haircut there.
The slow-motion shots were completely gratuitous.

definition: To lecture someone loudly and at length, often aggressively; or the long, ranting speech itself.
examples: The coach *harangued* the team for twenty minutes at half-time.
I got a *harangue* about leaving the lights on.
hook: Old French arenge — probably from a Germanic word for a ring of people gathered to listen.
openers: Please don't harangue me about the gym, I know.
I got harangued by a guy on the train about crypto.
Mum gave me a full harangue about my car's service history.

definition: Someone who doesn't belong to a widely held religion (dated, offensive in its original sense); now often used jokingly for someone uncivilised.
examples: Missionaries set out to convert the *heathens*.
You put milk in before the tea? You *heathen*.
hook: Old English hǣthen — possibly 'heath-dweller', someone living far from the Christian towns.
openers: You eat pizza with a knife and fork? Heathen.
Only a heathen skips the credits scene.

definition: Overly theatrical or dramatic in behaviour, especially to get attention.
examples: Her *histrionic* sobbing over a parking ticket was a bit much.
Spare me the *histrionics* — just tell me what happened.
hook: Latin histrio, 'actor'.
openers: Bit histrionic for a papercut, don't you think?
Spare me the histrionics, it's one missed bus.
The cat is being very histrionic about dinner being late.

definition: A very small human or human-like creature, especially one supposedly created by alchemy; also a map of the body drawn in the brain.
examples: Medieval alchemists claimed they could grow a *homunculus* in a flask.
The sensory *homunculus* has huge hands and lips.
hook: Latin 'little man' — homo 'man' + a diminutive ending.

definition: To drink, especially alcohol; or to absorb ideas or knowledge.
examples: Rather a lot was *imbibed* at the wedding.
She *imbibed* her grandfather's love of jazz.
hook: Latin imbibere, 'to drink in'.
openers: Will you be imbibing tonight or driving?
I imbibed far too much coffee before that exam.
Shall we go imbibe something at the pub?

definition: Without any faults or mistakes; perfect.
examples: Her timing was *impeccable*.
He's always *impeccably* dressed.
hook: Latin in- 'not' + peccare 'to sin' — literally 'unable to sin'. Same root as peccadillo.
openers: Your timing is impeccable — I just took the pizza out.
Impeccable parallel park.
Her taste in music is impeccable.

definition: Helplessness or lack of power to change things (also used medically for erectile dysfunction).
examples: The protesters raged at their *impotence* against the government.
I watched with *impotent* fury as the tram pulled away.
hook: Latin impotentia, 'lack of power'.
openers: The impotent rage of watching your Uber cancel.
There's a special impotence in shouting at the TV.

definition: Official approval or a stamp of endorsement from someone in authority.
examples: The plan went ahead with the board's *imprimatur*.
The restaurant has the *imprimatur* of every food critic in town.
hook: Latin 'let it be printed' — the Catholic Church's licence to publish a book.
openers: Do we have your imprimatur to order Thai?
This playlist has my mum's imprimatur, so you know it's wholesome.

definition: Rude, disrespectful cheekiness.
examples: The *impudence* of that kid, answering back like that.
He *impudently* helped himself to my chips.
hook: Latin impudens, 'shameless' — in- 'not' + pudere 'to be ashamed'.
openers: The impudence of this magpie, eating off my plate.
Don't be impudent, I'm still older than you.
What impudence — he took my parking spot.

definition: Clear, sharp and direct in thinking or expression; getting straight to the heart of a matter.
examples: She asked an *incisive* question that changed the whole discussion.
His *incisive* review was short but devastating.
hook: Latin incidere, 'to cut into' — the same root as incisor teeth.
openers: That's an incisive point — I hadn't thought of it.
Her feedback is always incisive, which is terrifying.
Very incisive analysis of my love life, thank you.

definition: Never seeming to get tired; persistently energetic.
examples: The *indefatigable* volunteers worked through the night.
She *indefatigably* answered every question.
hook: Latin in- 'not' + defatigare 'to tire out'.
openers: Your energy is indefatigable — how are you still dancing?
The kids are indefatigable today.
He's indefatigable when it comes to finding a bargain.

definition: Trying too hard to win someone's approval or favour.
examples: He gave the boss an *ingratiating* smile.
She laughed *ingratiatingly* at every one of his jokes.
hook: Latin in gratiam, 'into favour'.
openers: That was a very ingratiating compliment — what do you want?
The dog's being very ingratiating now that I'm holding a sausage.
Stop trying to ingratiate yourself with my parents.

definition: Insulting, abusive or strongly critical language.
examples: The comment section was a stream of *invective*.
He let loose a torrent of *invective* at the referee.
hook: Latin invehi, 'to attack with words' — literally 'to carry oneself against'.
openers: The invective coming from the couch during the footy was impressive.
My GPS got a lot of invective on that drive.

definition: Pleasantly lazy, slow and relaxed.
examples: We spent a *languorous* afternoon by the pool.
She gave a *languorous* stretch and went back to sleep.
hook: Latin languere, 'to be faint, weak' — the same root as languish.
openers: I'm planning a very languorous Sunday.
Look at the cat — the most languorous creature alive.

definition: Showing open or offensive sexual desire.
examples: He gave her a *lascivious* wink.
The novel was banned for its *lasciviousness*.
hook: Latin lascivia, 'playfulness, wantonness'.
openers: The way you're looking at that cheesecake is downright lascivious.
Bit of a lascivious description of a sandwich, that.

definition: A state of physical or mental tiredness and lack of energy.
examples: A strange *lassitude* came over him after lunch.
The summer heat brought a general *lassitude* to the office.
hook: Latin lassus, 'weary'.
openers: Post-lunch lassitude has hit me hard.
There's a real Sunday-afternoon lassitude in here.

definition: To look at someone in an unpleasant, suggestive or sly way.
examples: A man at the bar *leered* at her all night.
He gave a knowing *leer*.
hook: Old English hlēor, 'cheek' — glancing sideways over the cheek.
openers: Stop leering at my fries, get your own.
The dog's leering at the barbecue again.

definition: Ignoring accepted rules, especially about sex; promiscuous and unrestrained.
examples: The court was famous for its *licentious* parties.
Critics called the film *licentious* and vulgar.
hook: Latin licentia, 'freedom' — taking too much licence.
openers: That's a licentious amount of hot sauce.
Schoolies is basically a week of licentious behaviour.

definition: To perform a lobotomy on; figuratively, to make someone or something dull, passive or stupid.
examples: Hours of scrolling leave me feeling *lobotomized*.
The edit *lobotomized* the script.
hook: Greek lobos 'lobe' + tomē 'cutting'.
openers: Reality TV absolutely lobotomizes me.
I feel lobotomized after that three-hour meeting.
Don't let the algorithm lobotomize you.

definition: The craft of knotting cord or string into decorative patterns, like plant hangers.
examples: Her flat is full of plants in *macrame* hangers.
The 70s *macrame* trend is back.
hook: Turkish makrama 'napkin', from Arabic miqrama 'embroidered veil'. Also spelled macramé.

definition: Generous and forgiving, especially towards a rival or someone less powerful.
examples: She was *magnanimous* in victory and praised her opponent.
It was *magnanimous* of him to admit he was wrong.
hook: Latin magnus 'great' + animus 'soul' — 'great-souled'.
openers: I'll be magnanimous and let you have the last slice.
Very magnanimous of you to forgive me for being right.
Try to be magnanimous if we win tonight.

definition: Seeing the world in simple terms of good versus evil, with no grey areas.
examples: The film has a *Manichean* view of heroes and villains.
Politics has become depressingly *Manichean*.
hook: From Mani, a 3rd-century Persian prophet who taught a cosmic war between light and darkness.
openers: You're being very Manichean about cats versus dogs.
It's not that Manichean — both sides have a point.

definition: Not telling the truth; lying.
examples: The ad's claims were frankly *mendacious*.
His *mendacity* finally caught up with him.
hook: Latin mendax, 'lying'.
openers: That 'five-minute walk' on the listing was mendacious.
The mendacious weather app said it wouldn't rain.
You mendacious little liar, you said you'd saved me some.

definition: A beggar; or a member of a religious order that lives on charity.
examples: *Mendicant* friars travelled from town to town.
A *mendicant* sat by the temple gate.
hook: Latin mendicare, 'to beg'.

definition: A member of a Protestant Christian group known for simple living and pacifism.
examples: The *Mennonite* community runs a market every Saturday.
hook: Named after Menno Simons, a 16th-century Dutch Anabaptist leader.

definition: Crying weakly, like a baby or a kitten; whiny.
examples: A *mewling* kitten was stuck in the drain.
He's a *mewling* complainer.
hook: Imitative — it sounds like the weak cry it describes, like 'mew'.
openers: Stop mewling, it's just a cold.
I was a mewling wreck after that movie.

definition: A small place, group or situation that reflects the features of something much larger.
examples: The school is a *microcosm* of the wider community.
Our group chat is a *microcosm* of internet culture.
hook: Greek mikros kosmos, 'little world'.
openers: This share house is a microcosm of society.
Bunnings on a Sunday is a microcosm of Australia.
The office kitchen is a microcosm of every workplace drama.

definition: Relating to microliths — tiny flaked stone blades made by prehistoric people.
examples: Archaeologists found *microlithic* tools at the site.
The *microlithic* blades were set into wooden handles.
hook: Greek mikros 'small' + lithos 'stone'.

definition: Modern conveniences in a home, like a dishwasher, heating or Wi-Fi (informal).
examples: The cottage is rustic but has all the *mod cons*.
No *mod cons* — not even a microwave.
hook: Short for 'modern conveniences' — 1930s British estate-agent jargon.
openers: This Airbnb has all the mod cons — there's even a pizza oven.
Camping without any mod cons? Not for me.
No dishwasher? Where are the mod cons?

definition: Relating to the biological processes that give an organism or tissue its shape.
examples: The study focused on *morphogenic* signals in the embryo.
Turing proposed a *morphogenic* model to explain a leopard's spots.
hook: Greek morphē 'shape' + genesis 'origin'.

definition: Made up of very different, mismatched people or things.
examples: A *motley* crew of volunteers turned up to help.
The flat was furnished with a *motley* collection of op-shop finds.
hook: Originally the multicoloured patchwork costume of a court jester.
openers: What a motley crew we've assembled for trivia.
My fridge contains a motley assortment of condiments.
Our five-a-side team is a motley bunch.

definition: A famous cabaret in Paris, opened in 1889 and known for the cancan.
examples: Toulouse-Lautrec painted the dancers of the *Moulin Rouge*.
hook: French 'Red Mill' — after the red windmill on its roof.

definition: Of many different kinds; having great variety.
examples: Her *multifarious* interests include beekeeping and jazz.
The job involves *multifarious* responsibilities.
hook: Latin multifarius, 'manifold, in many places'.
openers: My reasons for not going to the gym are multifarious.
The multifarious uses of a butter knife — screwdriver, letter opener...

definition: The belly button. 'Navel-gazing' means self-absorbed overthinking.
examples: Less *navel*-gazing, more doing.
hook: Old English nafela.

definition: A light, thin, often see-through dressing gown or nightdress.
examples: She came down to breakfast in a silk *negligee*.
The vintage shop had a rack of lace *negligees*.
hook: French négligé, 'neglected' — i.e. casually, not fully dressed.

definition: An outdated and offensive racial category from 19th-century anthropology.
examples: The old textbook still used the term *negroid*, long since discredited.
hook: From discredited racial science; avoid using it.

definition: Having no equal; unrivalled. (As a noun, also tiny sugar sprinkles.)
examples: She's a *nonpareil* storyteller.
The cake was covered in rainbow *nonpareils*.
hook: French non 'not' + pareil 'equal' — without equal.
openers: Your nan's scones are nonpareil.
As a procrastinator, I'm nonpareil.

definition: So surprised or confused that you don't know how to react. (Often misused to mean 'unbothered'.)
examples: She was *nonplussed* when he proposed at the dentist's.
The question left the candidate completely *nonplussed*.
hook: Latin non plus, 'no more' — a state where nothing more can be said or done.
openers: I was totally nonplussed when he showed up in a tux.
The dog looked nonplussed by the vacuum cleaner.
Honestly nonplussed by that plot twist.

definition: An official authorised to witness signatures and certify legal documents.
examples: You'll need to get the form signed in front of a *notary*.
The *notary* stamped and signed each page of the will.
hook: Latin notarius, 'secretary, shorthand writer'.

definition: Deep respect, or a gesture of it such as a bow or curtsy.
examples: The courtiers made *obeisance* to the king.
Every new manager pays *obeisance* to the founder's vision.
hook: Old French obeissance, 'obedience'.
openers: We must pay obeisance to the coffee machine before anything else.
The cat demands obeisance every morning at 6.

definition: A person aged between 80 and 89.
examples: My grandad is a very active *octogenarian*.
The marathon's oldest finisher was an *octogenarian*.
hook: Latin octogenarius, 'containing eighty'.
openers: I've got the knees of an octogenarian.
That octogenarian at the pool swims faster than me.
Nan's turning into a very sassy octogenarian.

definition: Too eager to tell people what to do, especially in a petty, self-important way.
examples: An *officious* attendant insisted we move our towels.
His *officiousness* made the meeting drag on.
hook: Latin officiosus, 'obliging, dutiful' — dutiful to an annoying degree.
openers: The car-park guy was very officious about the white line.
Sorry to be officious, but the bins go out tonight.
Don't get officious about the roster, it's one shift.

definition: Involving a lot of effort, difficulty or responsibility.
examples: The paperwork for the visa was *onerous*.
They found the loan terms too *onerous*.
hook: Latin onus, 'burden' — as in 'the onus is on you'.
openers: Filling in this form is unnecessarily onerous.
Moving house is so onerous.
Not an onerous task — just grab some milk on the way.

definition: Wild, unrestrained and frenzied, like an orgy.
examples: The film ends in an *orgiastic* feast.
The crowd erupted in *orgiastic* celebration.
hook: Greek orgia, 'secret rites' — originally the worship of Dionysus.

definition: Writing, speech or entertainment that is bland, simplistic and lacking substance.
examples: The speech was forgettable *pablum*.
Most corporate newsletters are pure *pablum*.
hook: From Pablum, a bland 1930s baby cereal — itself from Latin pabulum, 'food, fodder'.
openers: That motivational post was such pablum.
This playlist is inoffensive pablum, but it'll do for dinner.

definition: An enthusiastic expression of praise, in words or song.
examples: The review was a *paean* to the chef's genius.
The song is a *paean* to summer in Sydney.
hook: Greek paian — a hymn of thanks to Apollo the healer.
openers: Sorry, I'm about to deliver a paean to this lasagne.
His speech was basically a paean to his dog.

definition: A Spanish rice dish cooked in a wide pan with saffron, seafood and/or meat.
examples: We shared a huge *paella* by the beach.
hook: Valencian for 'frying pan', from Latin patella, 'small pan'.

definition: A manuscript written over an earlier, partly erased text; or anything with visible layers of its past.
examples: The old city is a *palimpsest* of Roman, medieval and modern streets.
Scholars found a lost text of Archimedes beneath a medieval *palimpsest*.
hook: Greek palin 'again' + psēstos 'scraped' — parchment scraped clean and reused.
openers: This wall is a palimpsest of fifty years of band posters.
My whiteboard is a palimpsest of half-erased to-do lists.

definition: The belief that God is present in everything in the universe but also extends beyond it.
examples: Unlike pantheism, *panentheism* holds that God is more than the universe.
Some mystics describe their faith as a form of *panentheism*.
hook: Greek pan 'all' + en 'in' + theos 'god' — 'all in God'.

definition: A small metal drinking cup or pan (British/Australian, old-fashioned).
examples: The drover drank his tea from a battered *pannikin*.
Each swagman carried a billy and a *pannikin*.
hook: Simply 'pan' + the diminutive -kin: a little pan.

definition: As a side comment, as if in brackets.
examples: *Parenthetically*, she mentioned she'd quit her job.
He added *parenthetically* that the car had no brakes.
hook: Greek parenthesis, 'putting in beside'.
openers: Parenthetically, the milk's off — don't drink it.
And, parenthetically, I was right about the restaurant.
I'll mention parenthetically that you owe me twenty bucks.

definition: Having a large, sticking-out stomach.
examples: He's grown a bit *paunchier* since the wedding.
A *paunchy* middle-aged man was asleep in the deckchair.
hook: Old French panche, 'belly'.
openers: I'm getting paunchy — time to stop the second dessert.
Winter makes everyone a bit paunchier.
Look at the paunchy little cat.

definition: A short passage taken from a longer text, especially one read from the Bible during a service.
examples: The sermon focused on a single *pericope* from Luke.
Each week the lectionary sets a new *pericope* for the sermon.
hook: Greek perikopē, 'a cutting around' — a section cut out of a text.

definition: Light, teasing, witty conversation or banter.
examples: The dinner was all gossip and *persiflage*.
Under the *persiflage*, he was clearly hurt.
hook: French persifler, 'to banter' — from siffler, 'to whistle'.
openers: Enough persiflage, let's actually order.
I come to these drinks for the persiflage, not the beer.

definition: Childishly sulky or bad-tempered when you don't get your way.
examples: He gave a *petulant* shrug and stormed off.
Her *petulance* ruined the dinner.
hook: Latin petulans, 'impudent' — from petere, 'to aim at, attack'.
openers: Don't be petulant, you can pick the movie next time.
The cat is being petulant because I moved her blanket.
That was a very petulant email.

definition: The study of the history and development of languages, especially through old texts.
examples: Tolkien was a professor of *philology* at Oxford.
Her degree in classical *philology* meant reading Homer in Greek.
hook: Greek philologia, 'love of words'.

definition: Deeply religious; or making a show of being morally superior.
examples: His *pious* grandmother went to mass every day.
Spare me the *pious* lecture about recycling.
hook: Latin pius, 'dutiful'.
openers: Bit pious coming from someone who had three desserts.
Don't get pious about my screen time.
He's gone very pious since he started running.

definition: Of or like a pig.
examples: He had small, *porcine* eyes.
The dog gave a *porcine* snort.
hook: Latin porcus, 'pig' — the same root as pork.
openers: The snoring from the next room is distinctly porcine.
I made some porcine noises at that buffet.

definition: All future generations of people.
examples: The letters were kept for *posterity*.
*Posterity* will judge whether we acted in time.
hook: Latin posterus, 'coming after'.
openers: Take a photo of this pavlova for posterity.
I'm screenshotting that text for posterity.
Let posterity record that I called it first.

definition: Concerned with actual use rather than theory; sensible and realistic.
examples: We need a *practical* solution, not a perfect one.
hook: Greek praktikos, 'fit for action'.

definition: Having or showing knowledge of events before they happen.
examples: Her warning about the housing market proved *prescient*.
The novel's *prescience* about smartphones is eerie.
hook: Latin praescire, 'to know beforehand' — prae + scire (as in science).
openers: Bringing an umbrella was very prescient of you.
That joke last week turned out to be weirdly prescient.
How prescient — I just texted you.

definition: To avoid giving a direct answer; to speak evasively.
examples: When asked about the money, he *prevaricated*.
Stop *prevaricating* and tell me what happened.
hook: Latin praevaricari, 'to walk crookedly' — like a ploughman who won't plough a straight line.
openers: Stop prevaricating — did you eat my leftovers or not?
He prevaricated for ten minutes before admitting he forgot.
No prevaricating: pub or home?

definition: Forcing things to fit a rigid system, regardless of individual differences.
examples: The school's *Procrustean* timetable ignores how kids actually learn.
They applied a *Procrustean* rule to every case.
hook: Procrustes, a Greek bandit who stretched or chopped his guests' legs to fit his iron bed.
openers: The new expense policy is downright Procrustean.
These airline seats are Procrustean — nobody fits.

definition: Recklessly wasteful with money or resources; or living a wild, immoral life.
examples: The council was accused of *profligate* spending.
His *profligacy* left the family broke.
hook: Latin profligare, 'to strike down, ruin'.
openers: Ordering two entrées is profligate, but let's do it.
My profligate Uber Eats habit has to stop.

definition: An ancestor; or the person or thing that started something.
examples: Punk was the *progenitor* of grunge.
Their *progenitors* arrived on the First Fleet.
hook: Latin progignere, 'to beget'.
openers: You're the progenitor of this group chat — fix it.
Mum's the progenitor of our family's competitive streak.

definition: A forecast of how something, especially an illness, is likely to turn out.
examples: The doctor's *prognosis* was good.
The *prognosis* for the project is not great.
hook: Greek prognōsis, 'foreknowledge'.
openers: What's the prognosis on dinner — are we eating at nine?
The prognosis for my plants is grim.
Prognosis for the game: we lose by twenty.

definition: Working-class people, especially those who earn wages (a Marxist term).
examples: Marx predicted the *proletariat* would rise up.
As a lowly intern I'm firmly in the *proletariat*.
hook: Latin proletarius — Rome's lowest class, who served the state only by having children (proles).
openers: Business class? Some of us are proletariat, mate.
The proletariat demands a longer lunch break.

definition: Lying face down on the ground; or completely overcome and helpless.
examples: The pilgrims lay *prostrate* before the altar.
She was *prostrate* with grief.
hook: Latin prosternere, 'to throw down in front'. (Not to be confused with prostate.)
openers: After the hike I was prostrate on the couch for hours.
The heat has left me utterly prostrate.

definition: Eager to argue or fight; aggressive.
examples: He has a *pugnacious* style of debating.
The terrier lifted its chin *pugnaciously*.
hook: Latin pugnax, 'fond of fighting' — from pugnus 'fist' (as in pugilist).
openers: Why so pugnacious this morning? Have a coffee.
That little dog is incredibly pugnacious.
Bit of a pugnacious email, maybe soften it?

definition: Seemingly or partly but not really, as in quasi-official.
examples: It's a *quasi*-government body.
hook: Latin 'as if'.

definition: Lying down or leaning back.
examples: He rode a *recumbent* bike to work.
A *recumbent* statue lay on the tomb.
hook: Latin recumbere, 'to lie back' — related to incumbent.
openers: I'll be recumbent on the couch if anyone needs me.
My preferred position for watching the cricket is recumbent.

definition: To formally give up a claim, belief or habit.
examples: She *renounced* her citizenship.
He *renounced* sugar for Lent.
hook: Latin renuntiare, 'to announce against, protest'.
openers: I hereby renounce all carbs. Until Friday.
I'm renouncing social media for the week.
Did you renounce your loyalty to that café?

definition: Quick, witty conversation full of clever replies.
examples: The show is famous for its sharp *repartee*.
Their *repartee* across the dinner table was hilarious.
hook: French repartie, 'a reply' — originally a fencing term for a return thrust.
openers: Your repartee is wasted on this group chat.
I can't keep up with your repartee before coffee.
Great repartee with the waiter — he loved you.

definition: An unprincipled person who behaves badly (often used affectionately).
examples: My uncle is a lovable old *reprobate*.
The bar was full of *reprobates* at 2am.
hook: Latin reprobare, 'to disapprove' — originally someone rejected by God.
openers: You old reprobate — you ate the whole cheesecake?
Our neighbour's a charming reprobate.
Which reprobate left the gate open?

definition: A person who owns and runs a restaurant. (Note: no 'n'.)
examples: The *restaurateur* greeted every table personally.
The *restaurateur* opened a second venue across the road.
hook: French, from restaurer 'to restore' — a restaurant first meant a restoring broth.
openers: She's a successful restaurateur — three places in the city.
Fun fact: restaurateur has no 'n' in it.

definition: Able to remember facts easily; or able to hold on to something like heat or water.
examples: She has a *retentive* memory for birthdays.
The soil is very *retentive* of moisture.
hook: Latin retinere, 'to hold back'.
openers: You have a scarily retentive memory for embarrassing stories.
My brain isn't very retentive after midnight.

definition: An old-fashioned term for pain and stiffness in the joints and muscles.
examples: Grandpa's *rheumatism* plays up in the cold.
The damp cottage did nothing for her *rheumatism*.
hook: Greek rheuma, 'flow' — ancient doctors blamed aches on bad fluids flowing through the body.

definition: Excessively sweet or sentimental.
examples: The movie's ending was unbearably *saccharine*.
She gave a *saccharine* smile that didn't reach her eyes.
hook: Latin saccharum, 'sugar'. (Saccharin, no 'e', is the sweetener.)
openers: That ad was so saccharine I need a dentist.
Bit saccharine, this playlist.
Don't give me that saccharine smile.

definition: Relating to priests or the priesthood.
examples: He wore his *sacerdotal* robes to the ceremony.
The ceremony was full of *sacerdotal* pomp and incense.
hook: Latin sacerdos, 'priest' — from sacer, 'holy'.

definition: Having good judgement and practical wisdom.
examples: Her *sagacious* advice saved us a fortune.
The old dog gave a *sagacious* look.
hook: Latin sagax, 'keen-scented, shrewd' — like a hound on a trail.
openers: Very sagacious of you to book the table early.
Ask Dad — he's oddly sagacious about cars.
A sagacious decision, leaving before the rain.

definition: (Of skin) an unhealthy yellowish or pale-brown colour.
examples: He looked *sallow* after weeks indoors.
Her face grew *sallower* as the illness wore on.
hook: Old English salo, 'dusky, dark'.
openers: I look so sallow under these office lights.
You're looking a bit sallow — have you been outside this week?

definition: Wise or intelligent (often used ironically).
examples: The *sapient* elders of the village were consulted.
Are we sure the octopus isn't *sapient*?
hook: Latin sapere, 'to be wise' — as in Homo sapiens.

definition: The feeling of being completely full or satisfied, sometimes to excess.
examples: Protein increases your sense of *satiety*.
We ate to the point of *satiety*.
hook: Latin satis, 'enough' — the same root as satisfy and sated.
openers: I have reached total satiety. No dessert.
This pasta has no satiety point — I could eat it forever.

definition: Obsessed with or about excrement; toilet humour.
examples: The comedy relies on *scatological* jokes.
Kids love *scatological* humour.
hook: Greek skōr (skat-), 'dung'.
openers: The group chat has gone fully scatological again.
My nephew's humour is entirely scatological.

definition: Pleasure felt at someone else's misfortune.
examples: I felt a twinge of *schadenfreude* when his flashy car got a ticket.
The internet runs on *schadenfreude*.
hook: German Schaden 'harm' + Freude 'joy'.
openers: Pure schadenfreude watching the tailgater get pulled over.
Is it schadenfreude if I'm glad your team lost?
Bit of schadenfreude seeing him slip on the dance floor.

definition: The system of medieval philosophy and theology based on logic and the authority of ancient texts; or excessive hair-splitting.
examples: Thomas Aquinas is the giant of medieval *scholasticism*.
Renaissance humanists mocked *scholasticism* for arguing over angels on pinheads.
hook: Latin scholasticus, 'learned' — the 'schoolmen' of medieval universities.

definition: Belittling or humiliating yourself, often excessively.
examples: His apology turned into an act of grovelling *self-abasement*.
There's no need for such *self-abasement* over a typo.
hook: Old French abaissier, 'to lower'.
openers: Enough self-abasement — the cake looks fine.
Your apology text was a masterpiece of self-abasement.

definition: A tomb, especially one cut into rock or built of stone.
examples: The knight was laid to rest in a stone *sepulchre*.
The silence of the empty church felt like a *sepulchre*.
hook: Latin sepulcrum, from sepelire, 'to bury'.

definition: Very serious, strict or harsh.
examples: It was the *severest* drought in a century.
hook: Latin severus, 'strict'.

definition: Having had hair or wool cut off; or (shorn of) stripped of something.
examples: The sheep looked tiny once *shorn*.
*Shorn* of its special effects, the film is quite dull.
hook: The past participle of shear.
openers: Shorn of the fancy sauce, it's just chicken and rice.
Fresh haircut — I feel very shorn.

definition: Having sharp judgement and good practical sense, especially about money or people.
examples: She's a *shrewd* negotiator.
That was the *shrewdest* investment he ever made.
hook: Middle English shrewe, 'wicked person' — it originally meant malicious, like a shrew.
openers: Shrewd move, buying the tickets before the price went up.
Your nan's a shrewd card player — watch her.
That was shrewdly done.

definition: Relating to or resembling apes or monkeys.
examples: He swung across the monkey bars with *simian* ease.
The film's *simian* villain was surprisingly sympathetic.
hook: Latin simia, 'ape'.
openers: Your rock-climbing is impressively simian.
The kids have gone full simian on the playground.

definition: Very informal words and phrases used by a particular group.
examples: 'Arvo' is Australian *slang* for afternoon.
hook: 18th-century English, origin unknown.

definition: Extreme self-centredness; or the philosophical idea that only your own mind is sure to exist.
examples: His *solipsism* means every story somehow ends up being about him.
Social media can encourage a kind of *solipsism*.
hook: Latin solus 'alone' + ipse 'self'.
openers: That was a very solipsistic way to describe a group trip.
Peak solipsism: reviewing a restaurant by only talking about yourself.

definition: A social club for female university students, especially in the US.
examples: She joined a *sorority* in her first year at college.
hook: Latin soror, 'sister'.

definition: In a quiet voice, so as not to be overheard.
examples: 'He's lying,' she said *sotto voce*.
They exchanged *sotto voce* comments during the speech.
hook: Italian 'under voice'.
openers: Sotto voce: I think the groom's crying.
She muttered something sotto voce about the speeches being too long.
Say it sotto voce, the boss is right there.

definition: A very small amount or slight trace of something.
examples: Add a *soupçon* of chilli to the sauce.
There was a *soupçon* of sarcasm in his reply.
hook: French for 'suspicion' — just a suspicion of something.
openers: Just a soupçon of milk in my tea, please.
I detect a soupçon of jealousy.
A soupçon more wine wouldn't hurt.

definition: Happening in irregular bursts; or caused by muscle spasms.
examples: My gym attendance is *spasmodic* at best.
There was *spasmodic* gunfire through the night.
hook: Greek spasmos, 'convulsion'.
openers: The Wi-Fi's been spasmodic all day.
My motivation is spasmodic — very on, very off.

definition: An underlying layer or surface on which something grows or is built; in chemistry, the substance an enzyme acts on.
examples: The mushrooms grow on a *substrate* of straw.
Silicon is the *substrate* for most microchips.
hook: Latin substratum, 'strewn beneath'.

definition: Achieving what you set out to do.
examples: The launch was a huge *success*.
hook: Latin successus, 'an outcome' — from succedere, 'to come after'.

definition: Splendid, luxurious and obviously expensive.
examples: The hotel suite was *sumptuous*.
She cooked a *sumptuous* feast for twelve.
hook: Latin sumptus, 'expense'.
openers: This toastie is sumptuous, honestly.
What a sumptuous spread — you didn't have to.
Sumptuous couch — I'm never getting up.

definition: To split or break something apart (literary).
examples: The war *sundered* families.
The friendship was *sundered* by a single argument.
hook: Old English sundrian — it survives in 'asunder'.
openers: Pineapple on pizza has sundered this household.
Nothing will sunder me from this couch.

definition: An unnecessarily large amount; more than is needed.
examples: There was a *superfluity* of chairs and not enough tables.
The essay suffers from a *superfluity* of adjectives.
hook: Latin superfluere, 'to overflow'.
openers: We have a superfluity of tote bags in this house.
There's a superfluity of meetings this week.

definition: An excessive amount of something, often too much to enjoy.
examples: A *surfeit* of chocolate made everyone sick.
There's a *surfeit* of cooking shows on TV.
hook: Old French surfait, 'excess' — from surfaire, 'to overdo'.
openers: There's a surfeit of leftovers — take some home.
I've had a surfeit of Christmas songs this year.
Not a surfeit of parking around here, is there?

definition: Done secretly, because it wouldn't be approved of.
examples: She took a *surreptitious* photo of the celebrity.
He *surreptitiously* checked the score under the table.
hook: Latin surripere, 'to snatch secretly' — sub 'under' + rapere 'seize'.
openers: I saw that surreptitious second helping.
He's surreptitiously checking the cricket score.
Very surreptitious, hiding the chocolate behind the cereal.

definition: A substitute for someone or something; or a woman who carries a baby for another person.
examples: The dog became a *surrogate* child for them.
She acted as a *surrogate* for her sister.
hook: Latin surrogare, 'to elect as a substitute'.
openers: Decaf is a poor surrogate for real coffee.
My plants are surrogate pets.

definition: A young lover or suitor (old-fashioned or humorous); originally a country youth.
examples: Her latest *swain* turned up with roses.
Shepherds and *swains* fill the old pastoral poems.
hook: Old Norse sveinn, 'boy, servant' — the same root as boatswain.
openers: So who's your new swain?
Her swain brought her flowers again.

definition: Very severe or extreme, especially of cuts, fines or criticism (British).
examples: The government announced *swingeing* cuts to the arts.
He faced a *swingeing* fine for speeding.
hook: From the archaic verb swinge, 'to strike hard'.
openers: That was a swingeing parking fine.
The landlord's rent increase is swingeing.

definition: Combining different beliefs, cultures or styles into one.
examples: Cuban Santería is a *syncretic* religion.
The restaurant serves a *syncretic* mix of Korean and Mexican food.
hook: Greek synkrētismos — Plutarch's word for feuding Cretans uniting against a common enemy.

definition: Relating to tantra, a set of Hindu and Buddhist spiritual practices involving ritual and meditation.
examples: The temple is decorated with *tantric* symbols.
She studied *tantric* meditation in Nepal.
hook: Sanskrit tantra, 'loom, warp' — a woven doctrine.

definition: A fast, whirling Italian folk dance.
examples: The wedding guests danced a *tarantella*.
The band struck up a *tarantella* and everyone started spinning.
hook: From Taranto in Italy — folklore said the frenzied dance cured a tarantula bite.

definition: Excessive confidence or boldness; audacity.
examples: He had the *temerity* to criticise the chef's cooking — in his own restaurant.
Nobody had the *temerity* to tell her she was wrong.
hook: Latin temere, 'rashly, blindly'.
openers: You have the temerity to judge my driving?
The temerity of this cat, knocking my coffee over.
Who had the temerity to finish the milk?

definition: Relating to time; or relating to worldly affairs rather than spiritual ones.
examples: The bishop held both spiritual and *temporal* power.
The film plays with *temporal* jumps between decades.
hook: Latin tempus, 'time' — earthly time as opposed to eternity.
openers: My temporal awareness on weekends is non-existent.
That movie had too many temporal jumps for me.

definition: The period someone holds a job or position; or a permanent academic post.
examples: During her *tenure* as captain, the team never lost a final.
He finally got *tenure* at the university.
hook: Old French tenir, 'to hold'.
openers: During my tenure as house treasurer, nobody paid on time.
My tenure on this couch is permanent.

definition: An actor or actress (often used humorously).
examples: The local *thespians* put on Hamlet every year.
She's a born *thespian* — everything's a performance.
hook: From Thespis, a 6th-century BC Greek said to be the first actor.
openers: Alright, thespian, tone it down.
My little cousin's a natural thespian.
Very thespian reading of the menu there.

definition: Showing nervousness or a lack of confidence.
examples: A *timorous* knock came at the door.
His *timorousness* cost him the job.
hook: Latin timor, 'fear' — the same root as timid.
openers: That was a very timorous knock — come in!
Don't be timorous, just ask for the raise.

definition: An act that breaks a rule, law or moral code.
examples: His past *transgressions* came back to haunt him.
Eating in the library was a minor *transgression*.
hook: Latin transgredi, 'to step across' — stepping over a line.
openers: Leaving a pan to soak is not a transgression, it's a strategy.
I'll forgive your transgression if you buy lunch.

definition: Not permanent; lasting only a short time.
examples: Fame is *transitory*.
The *transitoriness* of youth is a theme of the poem.
hook: Latin transire, 'to go across, pass'.
openers: My enthusiasm for running is transitory.
Enjoy the clean kitchen — it's transitory.

definition: A dated term, often considered offensive, for a person who wears clothes associated with another gender; 'cross-dresser' is preferred.
examples: The novel uses the dated term *transvestite*.
hook: Latin trans 'across' + vestire 'to dress'.

definition: Two pence; used to mean a trivially small amount ('I don't care tuppence').
examples: I wouldn't give *tuppence* for his opinion.
The old sweets cost *tuppence* a bag.
hook: Simply 'two pence', said quickly.
openers: I don't care tuppence what the reviews say.
Here's my tuppence worth: get the bigger one.

definition: Having or like ulcers; figuratively, festering and corrupt.
examples: The patient had *ulcerous* sores on his legs.
An *ulcerous* resentment grew between them.
hook: Latin ulcus, 'sore'.

definition: Pure, with nothing added; complete and absolute.
examples: The concert was two hours of *unadulterated* joy.
That's *unadulterated* nonsense.
hook: Latin adulterare, 'to corrupt' — the same root as adultery.
openers: That's unadulterated rubbish and you know it.
This is unadulterated bliss — a Sunday with no plans.
Unadulterated chaos at the shops today.

definition: A mammal with hooves, such as a horse, deer or cow.
examples: Giraffes and pigs are both *ungulates*.
The national park is home to several species of *ungulate*.
hook: Latin ungula, 'hoof' — from unguis, 'nail'.

definition: Lending money at unreasonably high rates of interest.
examples: The payday lender's rates are basically *usury*.
Medieval law banned *usury*.
hook: Latin usura, 'use (of money)'.
openers: Twenty-five percent interest? That's usury.
Charging me a coffee for a two-dollar loan is pure usury.

definition: Designed to be useful rather than attractive; or based on the idea of the greatest good for the greatest number.
examples: The office furniture is grey and *utilitarian*.
From a *utilitarian* view, the bigger hospital saves more lives.
hook: Latin utilis, 'useful' — the philosophy of Bentham and Mill.
openers: My wardrobe is purely utilitarian.
It's not pretty, but it's utilitarian.
Very utilitarian lunch — rice, chicken, done.

definition: To keep changing your mind; to be indecisive.
examples: I *vacillated* between the two jobs for weeks.
Stop *vacillating* and pick a restaurant.
hook: Latin vacillare, 'to sway, totter'.
openers: I've been vacillating between pizza and Thai for twenty minutes.
Stop vacillating — just buy the shoes.
She vacillates every time we plan a trip.

definition: Lack of thought, intelligence or meaning; emptiness.
examples: The *vacuity* of the speech was astonishing.
He stared into space with total *vacuity*.
hook: Latin vacuus, 'empty' — the same root as vacuum.
openers: The vacuity of that reality show is impressive.
I'm in a state of post-exam vacuity.

definition: To give or assign value to something; to praise or treat something as worthy.
examples: The culture *valorises* hard work above all else.
The exhibition *valorises* everyday objects.
hook: French valoriser, from Latin valor, 'worth'.

definition: (Of veins) swollen, twisted and enlarged, usually in the legs.
examples: Standing all day gave her *varicose* veins.
Compression socks can ease *varicose* veins.
hook: Latin varix, 'dilated vein'.

definition: A type of popular theatre with a mix of comedy, singing, dancing and acts, especially in early-1900s America.
examples: Charlie Chaplin got his start in *vaudeville*.
The meeting turned into a *vaudeville* act.
hook: French, from 'vau de Vire' — satirical songs from the valley of Vire in Normandy.
openers: That press conference was pure vaudeville.
He's got a very vaudeville sense of humour.

definition: Open, uncultivated grassland in southern Africa.
examples: Herds of zebra grazed on the *veldt*.
The farm stretched out across the dry *veldt*.
hook: Afrikaans veld, 'field'.

definition: To regard with great respect and reverence.
examples: The old master is *venerated* by his students.
In some cultures, elders are deeply *venerated*.
hook: Latin venerari, 'to adore, revere' — related to Venus.
openers: You venerate that cast-iron pan more than your family.
Our house venerates the air-fryer.

definition: Speech or writing that uses too many words, or overly complicated ones.
examples: Cut the *verbiage* and get to the point.
The contract is buried in legal *verbiage*.
hook: French verbier, 'to chatter'.
openers: Strip out the verbiage and the email's one line.
Sorry for the verbiage, I'll get to the point.
So much corporate verbiage in that update.

definition: A small entrance hall or lobby just inside a building's front door.
examples: Leave your umbrellas in the *vestibule*.
We waited in the hotel *vestibule*.
hook: Latin vestibulum, 'entrance court'.
openers: Shoes off in the vestibule, please.
Meet you in the vestibule — it's freezing out here.

definition: Unwelcome changes of circumstance; the ups and downs of life.
examples: Their friendship survived the *vicissitudes* of thirty years.
The *vicissitudes* of the housing market make planning hard.
hook: Latin vicissitudo, 'change' — from vicis 'turn' (as in vice-captain).
openers: Ah, the vicissitudes of public transport.
We've survived the vicissitudes of share-house life.
Such are the vicissitudes of supporting this footy team.

definition: Wooden panelling on the lower part of a room's walls.
examples: The old dining room had oak *wainscoting*.
A mouse ran behind the *wainscoting*.
hook: Middle Dutch wagenschot, a kind of fine oak board.

definition: To choose not to insist on a right, rule or fee.
examples: The bank agreed to *waive* the late fee.
She *waived* her right to a lawyer.
hook: Anglo-Norman weyver, 'to abandon' — the same root as waif.
openers: Ask them to waive the delivery fee.
I'll waive my right to the front seat this time.
Can you waive the cover charge if we just have one drink?

definition: The state of being married (old-fashioned).
examples: They were joined in holy *wedlock*.
Born out of *wedlock*, he never knew his father.
hook: Old English wedlāc, 'pledge-giving' — nothing to do with a lock.
openers: Congrats on the impending wedlock.
Wedlock's suiting you — you look happy.

definition: An archaic insult meaning 'son of a whore'; used by Shakespeare for any contemptible person.
examples: 'Thou *whoreson* dog!' cries a character in King Lear.
hook: Literally 'whore's son' — one of Shakespeare's favourite insults.
